newsitem.title: HUNGARY: EXPECTED TRADE GAP GROWTH NOT WORRYING-HUNGARY MIN.
newsitem.headline: EXPECTED TRADE GAP GROWTH NOT WORRYING-HUNGARY MIN.

text.p: Hungary is unlikely to narrow its trade gap in 1997 and it is possible that the deficit will widen to $3 billion, the minister for trade, industry and tourism said on Monday.

"We expect imports to increase in 1997 at the same pace as exports or faster," Szabolcs Fazakas told a news conference. "We believe it is quite possible that the deficit would increase to $3 billion."
Hungary had a 1996 trade deficit of $2.7 billion, marginally higher than the 1995 trade gap, the ministry said in a statement.

In 1994, the deficit was $3.9 billion which together with the country's large budget deficit that year, dented investor confidence in the country and prompted the government to take a set of emergency measures in March, 1995.
Fazakas said, however, that the expected increase in the trade deficit is no cause for alarm.

"This is very different from what happened in 1994," he said. "The volume of both exports and imports has increased substantially since then, so this (the 1997 deficit) is relatively not that big. Also, the economy is much healthier now."
In 1994, exports stood at $10.7 billion, while in 1997 they are expected to increase by more than 10 percent from 1996's $16 billion, Fazakas said.
One of the reasons for the expected import increase in 1997 is Hungary's declining import duties.
A special, supplementary duty of eight percent that was one of the emergency measures of March, 1995 was reduced by two percentage points in 1996, the minister said.
This, together with reductions of various administrative fees, cut the costs of imports by five percent during last year, he added.
The supplementary duty is set to be reduced to four percent as of March 10 and is scheduled to be entirely eliminated in by the second half of this year.
In addition to lower duties, growing domestic demand is also going to boost imports in 1997, Fazakas said.
Prime Minister Gyula Horn said earlier that the real income of Hungarians is not expected to decrease in 1997 after two years of rapid decline.
